entries.title: Coders Say They Already Found Workarounds to Claude’s Invisible Watermarks
entries.summary: Anthropic announced last week it would include invisible watermarks in AI-generated content to comply with new EU rules. Within hours, overrides were being touted online.
entries.content:
Within four hours of Anthropic confirming that Claude models would globally embed invisible, machine-readable watermarks into any AI-generated content, developer Guillaume Meyer had published his override.

His code to remove watermarks from Claude-generated text has since gone viral on GitHub, has been bookmarked more than 20,000 times on X, and has drawn more than 100 contributors, with many more incorporating the technology into their own projects. “Anthropic is embedding watermarks in its Claude texts … the issue is practically history just one day later,” wrote one AI specialist, accompanied by an image of Meyer breaking out of chains and standing on crumpled EU and Anthropic flags.

Meyer and others started investigating how watermarking works after Anthropic announced last week that Claude would adopt it in order to comply with the European Union’s AI Act.

Some are trying to evade the watermarking because they disagree with the idea that all AI-generated content should be labeled as such, Meyer told WIRED, while others, including himself, say they simply relish the technical challenge. Freelance content writers and social media creators have also contacted Meyer asking for assistance using the code, he says.

The new rules, which came in earlier this month, stipulate that model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI must label synthetic audio, image, video, or text so that this material can be detected by a machine as AI-generated—or face fines of up to 3 percent of annual turnover. While the rules say providers cannot market circumvention tools, there is no legal restriction on independent tools.

“I'm not against transparency, and I'm all for content attribution,” says Meyer. “I just think watermarking in itself is a really bad solution, because it has major drawbacks and risks.” He is concerned about the risk of false positives and that the watermarking might not distinguish between light or heavy AI use, especially since, as a native French speaker, he often uses Claude and other AI tools like Grammarly to edit his writing. Using the watermark as evidence–when even Anthropic admits it can only generate a probability that the text has been touched by Claude–could lead to employers unfairly rejecting candidates or overblown accusations of researchers using artificial intelligence just because the detector flags it, he says.

Anthropic watermarks text invisibly by leaving a pattern in Claude’s choice of words and phrases that is indiscernible to a human reader but would be detectable by a machine that knows how to look for it. Because this influences Claude’s output, some users are concerned this will degrade the quality of Claude’s responses, though Anthtropic insists this won’t be the case. The technique, called SynthID, was developed by Google, which has been using it to watermark its AI-generated content since 2023. Computer scientist Scott Aaronson proposed a similar method when working at OpenAI but says the firm never deployed it because the company was worried that watermarks would put customers off its product.

Meyer’s removal method uses a non-watermarking large language model to generate multiple rewrites, swapping in synonyms and slightly reorganizing content. Of course, this relies on using other large language models which do not insert watermarks—possibly not a safe bet since 190 organizations—providers OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta among them—have signed the EU’s transparency code of practice. It remains to be seen how many of these laboratories are going to implement their watermarks, which must be included in all new models released from August and must be integrated into existing models by December.

While there’s no certainty this tool works until Anthropic releases the software it uses to detect a watermark, understanding the basic SynthID-text approach underpinning Claude’s watermarking makes them fairly sure the method works, says Wayne Pan, chief technology and cofounder at Silicon Valley–based sovereign AI startup Haimaker. He incorporated Meyer’s open-source tool into his platform because he similarly disliked the idea of Claude watermarking content even when it’s only been lightly edited and disagreed with the watermark being invisible to the user.

Other coders have developed their own removal tools: Software engineer Erik Hughes took 15 minutes to knock up a tool with Claude that removes invisible and look-alike characters, reorders sentences within paragraphs, and swaps several words for synonyms. Leon Chlon, a Visiting Fellow at the University of Oxford, says the watermarks can be removed by condensing Claude’s response, translating it into a dialect like Arabic, which has very different semantics compared to English, and then translating it back. Anthropic itself acknowledged that heavily edited, paraphrased, or translated content might not carry a watermark.

In a statement to WIRED, a spokesperson for Anthropic said: "We're adding marking to Claude's output to comply with the EU AI Act, and other labs are taking similar steps. It’s hard to identify AI-generated text, and this gives people better tools for identification. Text from supported Claude models, including output from Claude Code, will carry an invisible watermark, and it doesn't change the meaning, quality, or readability of Claude's responses. We also plan to ship a text-detection API so users can do more of this themselves.”

Anthropic says it’s working out how to implement watermark detection for text and plans to release a tool to do so soon—at which point developers will finally be able to see whether their methods are foolproof. It’s also continuing to work on improving the watermarking system. “I think they wanted to show that they're in good faith doing it,” says Pan, “but I don't think you can ever have a watermark that will withstand everything.”

entries.title: Google Pixel Watch 5 Review: More Health, More AI
entries.summary: With smarter gym tracking, new health alerts, and offline Gemini, the Pixel Watch 5 fine-tunes a winning formula—for a price.
entries.content:
Remains a stunning design. New Health Guardian features with proactive wellness insights. Strength Training experience is useful for gymgoers. Gemini now has offline functionality. Double the storage.

TIRED

AI watch faces feel gimmicky. Price has crept up. Active Band is still dull. Still no better charging ecosystem.

The Google Pixel Watch has always been a gorgeous smartwatch (minus the Active Band, which we’ve complained about ad nauseam). With Google Health Premium and Google Health Coach now part of the experience, it’s also one of the few smartwatches that feels equally capable as a fitness tracker and an everyday companion.

The Pixel Watch 5 takes a repairable model we already love and fine-tunes it, with most of the meaningful changes coming to Google’s health and fitness tools. Like the Fitbit Air, it leans further into proactive health insights. Most of our complaints about the Pixel Watch 4 remain, except that Gemini now has (some) offline functionality.

Smarter and Still Domed

Google says the Pixel Watch 5 is 20 percent faster than its predecessor, thanks to its upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip. CPU performance gets a 12 percent boost, and there's double the RAM. I didn’t notice a dramatic difference in speed compared to the Watch 4, but I also had few complaints to begin with. Scrolling is smooth, apps load and update quickly, and Gemini responds to voice commands without much lag.

The Pixel Watch maintains its domed design, which remains one of my favorite traits. The curved display makes information easy to glance at while giving the smartwatch a more approachable look. There were already plenty of watch faces to choose from, and Google has added two more, along with 11 complication styles.

You can also now use generative AI to create a custom face from a prompt. The customization is somewhat limited; you’re essentially choosing the font, but it was surprisingly responsive to my weirder requests. My Nickelodeon-themed prompt produced an orange face covered in slime, and brand-inspired prompts were decent at mimicking iconic fonts like Coca-Cola's. Still, I never landed on an AI-generated face I liked more than the defaults, so I went back to Digital Bold.

I tested the 45-mm model, and it’s the right choice if you want a larger display for readability and glanceability during workouts. But I previously used the 41-mm Watch 4, and I do prefer that size for my smaller wrists. Even with the smaller screen, notifications and workout stats are easy to read.

The Watch 5 features a larger battery than its predecessor, mainly to support new AI capabilities. For that reason, battery life remains similar, with Google estimating up to 40 hours. I get about 36 hours, which is still solid. What continues to impress me the most, though, is the fast charging, which delivers 15 hours of use in just 15 minutes. This is a game changer when I forget to charge it before heading out for a workout (which is often!). Google still hasn't introduced additional charging options or 3-in-1 or 2-in-1 docks for its Pixel portfolio (the Apple Watch has so many charging accessories), and we’re still patiently waiting.

It still comes with an Active Band (ugh), but there are new color options, including Fog, Canyon (exclusive to the 41-mm model), and Olive. Prices have also gone up, starting at $399 (41 mm) and $429 (45 mm). Similar to the Fitbit Air, there’s a Stephen Curry Special Edition, which comes with a water-repellent band for a total of $579.

More Ways to Track Your Health

Fitness tracking gets some of the biggest upgrades. The new Strength Training experience adds a workout builder, audio cues, rest timers, and the ability to track weights and reps. You can create a custom workout in the Google Health app, then have the watch guide you through each exercise and time your rest periods. You can also ask Google’s AI coach to build a workout based on a photo of your equipment.

Whether you’ll actually use all of this depends on your active lifestyle, but I can see it being particularly useful for someone new to the gym who wants a little structure that feels personal. I do appreciate that it syncs to the watch, so I can see rep counts and rest intervals without unlocking my phone.

Gemini is still one of Pixel Watch’s best features, and it can now tackle offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is handy if you tend to leave your phone at home on runs. The dual-band GPS is the same, but Google says route tracking is now twice as accurate in urban environments. It now accounts for atmospheric interference and multipath errors, which should help it maintain more accurate positioning around tall buildings. So far, I’ve had zero issues with route mapping in Chicago, and I can say the same for the previous model. I’m curious whether people in New York City might notice a bigger difference.

The Watch 5 retains several health features from its predecessors, including Loss of Pulse detection, ECG, and skin temperature tracking. It also introduces four Health Guardian tools that have undergone clinical validation and will be available in September: Insulin Resistance Trends, Blood Pressure Trends, Breathing Emergency Detection, and Sleep Breathing Quality Trends.

Insulin Resistance Trends analyzes weeks of physiological data to identify shifts in metabolic health without requiring a blood draw. The watch can also passively track pulse and motion patterns throughout the month to estimate blood pressure trends without manual calibration. Breathing Emergency Detection monitors blood oxygen levels for potentially dangerous drops and, if you become unresponsive, can automatically contact emergency services.

Lastly, Sleep Breathing Quality uses minute-by-minute variations in blood oxygen levels to understand your breathing patterns better while you sleep. Every morning, you’ll see how much of the night you spent with optimal breathing, along with a monthly assessment to recognize longer-term trends. Most of these Health Guardian features, except for Breathing Emergency Detection, are more useful for identifying patterns and should not be used for diagnosis. I wasn’t able to evaluate Health Guardian during testing, considering many of these features aren't available yet and they require a month of data before establishing meaningful trends.

On the topic of slumber, sleep tracking gets a refresh, too. Google says the Pixel Watch 5 is 15 percent more accurate at tracking sleep than its predecessor. There’s now a dedicated Bedtime Mode that silences notifications, disables the always-on display, simplifies the watch face, and adds a red tint designed to be easier on your eyes in the dark. If you enable the setting, the watch can also automatically pause media when it detects that you’ve fallen asleep.

Smart Wake Alarms aim to wake you during a 30-minute window when you’re in your lightest stage of sleep. This is one of those features that will depend on your personal preference. I value every last minute of sleep, and I find that Smart Wake inevitably wakes me earlier than I want. It’s also worth remembering that sleep-stage tracking is better as a way to identify long-term patterns than as a precise measurement, which makes me a little skeptical of Smart Wake’s accuracy.

Earlier this spring, Google launched the Fitbit Air, which was one of its first wearables built around Google Health Premium and Health Coach. The Pixel Watch 5 gets access to those same tools, too. Most of the insights are also locked behind the Premium subscription, so it really does feel like a necessary part of the experience. You do get three months free with the watch, at least.

The Watch 5 is Google’s best smartwatch, but many of the new software features will also be rolling out to the Watch 4. So if you need a smartwatch but you're feeling the pinch of the current economic crisis, you might be able to save some cash with last year's model.

Boutayna Chokrane is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering consumer products and online trends. She specializes in fitness equipment, beauty tech, apparel, and more. entries.title: Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: Smart Software, Small Upgrade
entries.summary: Google’s new voice typing is pure magic, but subpar gaming performance and a useless rear LED keep these flagships from true greatness.
entries.content:
Classy design. Bright, colorful screen. Nice improvements to the camera experience. Magic Capture can be useful. Gemini Intelligence is helpful, if limited. Rambler might be Google's best feature in years. Still the only major Android phones with Qi2 magnets.

TIRED

HiLight is pretty useless. Some graphics issues and generally unimpressive gaming performance in demanding titles. Battery life is just adequate.

There is one new feature on Google's Pixel 11 series that, I kid you not, caused my jaw to drop. It's an upgrade over one of my most-used Pixel features: voice-to-text.

I am a swipe typer, whizzing my finger across letters to form words instead of tapping each key individually. But I'm also heavily reliant on voice typing. Google's Pixel phones are far and away the best at it; more accurate at understanding my words than iPhones and Samsungs, not to mention sprinkling in punctuation at the right moments.

With the Pixel 11 devices, there's a new feature called Rambler—an upgraded, AI-powered voice-to-text feature—that is smarter than anything you've probably used before. Tap the microphone button on Gboard, and start talking. The Pixel will strip away the “ums” and “uhs,” and if you make a mistake and restate something, it won't bother to include that bit in your message, only keeping the parts it believes you want to convey. You can even ask it to add bullet points or an emoji to format your message, all in the same breath.

The accuracy of the voice-to-text is incredible, especially as you see it understand the mistakes, pauses, or vocal fillers. But what really made my eyes widen was speaking in my mother tongue, Malayalam. Rambler did a surprisingly great job at romanizing my words into English—a way I sometimes type to my family because I can't read or write the language. It's something I've never been able to do with a smartphone's voice-to-text function. To top it off, I asked it to translate the transcribed sentence into Malayalam, and it did the job. I fired off the messages to my Mom, and she said, “Very good.” High praise indeed.

These are the kinds of features that make a Pixel phone feel joyous to use. Smart, helpful everyday capabilities that can make a genuine impact on your day. Call Screen is another one of them, a feature Google pioneered that filters spam and robocalls and is now a staple in competing devices. Google Recorder is another I use every day, turning what was once a basic recording app into a powerful on-device transcription service.

Rambler, exclusive to the entire Pixel 11 range, may end up coming to older Pixel devices—Google hasn't shared details yet. It's not even restricted to the Pro devices, which is what I've been testing the past week.

Up to Eleven

The Pro Pixels this year are not a major leap over their predecessors. Many of the improvements are with the cameras—still a big reason to buy a Pixel—but there are some minor, welcome upgrades, like a scratch-resistant display coating, a brighter screen, more base storage, and faster charging. I quite like the all-glass camera bar, which looks especially elegant in the new colors (and most importantly, doesn't rock on a table).

HiLight is one of the big new exclusive features—unavailable on the base Pixel 11—and I'm disappointed to say that you're not missing much. This LED glows when your phone is face down and when you activate Gemini, so you know the assistant is listening, much like Google's new smart speaker; it can light up a specific color when someone calls you, allowing you to stay somewhat connected. Except there are only five colors to choose from.

If I want to set a HiLight color for more than five people in my Contacts app, I'll have to reuse colors, rendering the feature useless—it's baffling that there's no color wheel. While Google says HiLight will support text message notifications in the future, it's bizarre that this simple capability isn't available at launch. I'm all for weird, quirky features on smartphones, but HiLight is too limited to be useful. Maybe, in a few Pixel generations, it will disappear, much like the temperature sensor from three Pixels ago.

For the vast majority of Pixel owners, you won't run into any performance issues with Google's new Tensor G6 chip. But for the sliver of folks who want to dip into high-end gaming—and why shouldn't they? These are flagship phones that cost $1,099 and $1,299, respectively—prepare to be bummed. Standard games like Tennis Clash and Pako Forever ran without a hitch, but demanding titles like Zenless Zone Zero struggled to run smoothly. Worse was Genshin Impact, which gave me a purple screen that was impossible to play.

A Google spokesperson tells WIRED: “We are currently working with our partner HoYoverse to address this optimization issue on the Pixel 11. A fix is expected to be implemented in Genshin Impact's upcoming update.” In fairness, this graphical issue didn't happen in any other games I tried, even Zenless Zone Zero, another HoYoverse game.

Pixels have had this kind of suboptimal graphical performance for a long time, and it's becoming increasingly harder to ignore at these ever-increasing smartphone prices, especially when these issues aren't present on its peers. Will there ever be a Pixel with flagship-grade gaming performance?

Rambler is the breakout software feature for me this year, but Google is also highlighting Gemini Intelligence and “Proactive Assistance,” where Gemini will surface helpful actions. For example, my friend suggested getting dim sum this weekend, and when asked when to meet, a bubble popped up in the Messages app letting me quickly view my calendar without leaving the app. Then, when we settled on a time, another bubble popped up asking if I wanted to create the calendar event.

It all worked very smoothly, though Gemini struggled to understand that the restaurant's name was “Din Soup,” not Dim Sum. The bigger problem is that this kind of proactive assistance is largely available in the Messages app, which, unfortunately, is not my default messaging mode. When this becomes a system-wide capability that works in every app, I can see its utility.

Google has made some overall tweaks throughout the Pixel's interface that I think give it a stronger, more unique design language. I also do want to call out that these are still the only major Android phones with built-in Qi2 magnets—aka the magnetic back like MagSafe on the iPhone. I am all in on MagSafe accessories, whether that's my car dock or my mobile tripod, so it's indispensable to me.

Speaking of, battery life is rather unimpressive on both Pixel 11 Pro models. (The only difference between the pair is battery life and screen size.) I averaged four hours of screen-on time before the Pixel 11 Pro XL hit 20 percent, and roughly the same on the Pixel 11 Pro. Granted, I was downloading data over cellular, using Google Maps, and taking a lot of photos. I think average users will find it sufficient for a full day, but power users will undoubtedly need a top-up. Perhaps it's time for Google to consider denser batteries with silicon-carbon battery technology?

Camera Obscura

Do you really need 120X digital zoom? When you say it out loud, it sounds ridiculous, but then you look at the results, and it's hard not to be impressed. Yes, there are AI-generated pixels (anything past 30X zoom) filling in the gaps, which will be a nonstarter for many, but look how far away I am! It's actually quite a struggle to capture photos at that high level of zoom because the camera gets very shaky. Still, having access to this level of zoom means I am more comfortable zooming in to 30 or 50X, where the results are even better.

The two big hardware changes to the camera system are the new 50-megapixel main sensor and a new 48-MP telephoto zoom with 30 percent better light sensitivity. But the Tensor G6 chip is also powering many imaging improvements that should result in stronger photos overall.

First of all, I am happy to report that Google seems to have finally fixed Portrait mode. For too long, the Pixel's Portrait mode has struggled with hair, causing weird glitches or artifacts with rogue strands of hair at the edges of a person's head. It's not perfect now, but it's significantly better at detecting individual strands of hair and figuring out the best way to blur everything behind them.

Night Sight on these Pro devices is now Instant Night Sight, and is supposedly up to 4.5 times faster. I think Google may have jumped the gun on Instant because there's still a small pause when you hit the shutter button, and if you or your subject are moving slightly, it will still probably come out a little blurry. But it's certainly not as long of a pause as before, which makes low-light photography a smidge more forgiving to those kinds of smaller movements.

As someone who loves using the telephoto zoom on smartphone cameras, the 5X camera is excellent, delivering sharp, detailed images even at night. I took a handful of shots comparing these cameras with the iPhone 17 Pro, and I found Google did a better job replicating colors, though still slightly preferring cooler tones. The iPhone tended to make everything way warmer than it was in real life.

The nice thing is that Google finally gives you a little more control over how your photos look. Camera Looks, tucked away in the camera settings, lets you choose a different visual style. That might mean purposefully taking a worse photo, maybe with crushed highlights or lifted shadows, so your photos aren't this perfect slice of life, but imperfect and you. I seem to be gravitating to the Vanilla and Velvet looks the most.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, Portrait Mode

Another one of those features that makes everyday life a little easier—if you tend to shoot videos for a living like me—is Creator Suite. This mode in the Video tab of the camera app enables handy tools, like an audio visualizer, so you know your wireless mic is picking up your voice. But what I love most is the built-in teleprompter. It understands the cadence of your voice and will progress to the next line as you speak. It worked perfectly in my test run, and I'm excited to use it at the next big event I cover soon.

Finally, there's Magic Capture. It's a dedicated mode next to Photo and Video that is designed to make it so that you can just hold the phone up and it'll capture several photos on your behalf. You'll even get a 1080p video clip (though you can boost it to 4K using Google's Video Boost technology). The idea is that if you're singing happy birthday to your kid, your face isn't buried behind a phone, instead looking at the scene in real life while you have the phone held next to you capturing the moment.

I didn't have a special occasion to use it for this past week, but I did hold up the phone while my dog was playing with other pooches at the dog park and also to shoot scenes of volleyball at the park, and it did a pretty good job capturing photos that would otherwise have required more focus on my part. I just wish Magic Capture could change the lenses itself because right now that's something you have to pick manually. This feature seems ripe for Google's upcoming pair of smart glasses, considering you won't have to hold anything up at all.

All in all, the Pixel 11 Pro models are yet another strong entry that deliver the camera prowess expected of a Pixel and the software smarts. There are still some areas where Google needs to catch up with its competitors, namely graphical performance and battery life, especially if it's going to charge this much.

But it's also worth noting that you do not need to spend this much if you want a good phone. Google brings many of these smart capabilities down to its cheaper A-series phone, which also still has a class-leading camera and performance for the money, or you can get a very similar experience with the slightly cheaper Pixel 11.

(And by the way, I've completely written these last few paragraphs using Rambler.)

Julian Chokkattu is Senior Editor, Gear at WIRED, overseeing personal technology, gadgets, and gizmos. He has been reviewing consumer products for a decade, specializing in mobile—from smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches to smart glasses and virtual reality. This is his sixth year at WIRED. entries.title: Why Is It Absolute Hell to Buy a Movie Ticket Now?
entries.summary: Overwhelmed theater apps and a scarcity mindset around exclusive big-screen formats for blockbusters like Dune: Part Three and The Odyssey have led to the “concertification” of movies.
entries.content:
The conclusion to Denis Villeneuve’s epic Dune trilogy is still four months away, but the anticipation was palpable on Tuesday, the first day of ticket presales.

Theater chain apps suffered apparent outages as moviegoers waited in long virtual lines, hoping to finally glimpse a seat map with some empty spots left on it. In Manhattan, those who have grown mistrustful of this unreliable tech found time on a weekday morning to line up around the block at AMC Lincoln Square—hours before the box office opened. It was the third frenzied rush for blockbuster tickets in a few short weeks, following sky-high demand for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

Customers have been particularly keen to see these films on IMAX screens, with Dune: Part Three and The Odyssey also available in the even more exclusive IMAX 70mm format. Only 25 theaters in the US are capable of showing a film this way.

While directors and studios have embraced such premium screenings for tentpole releases (not least because those tickets are more expensive), the rarity of theaters equipped for them has contributed to a scarcity mindset. People are so bent on experiencing these movies in the “best” possible way, and, if not on opening night, as soon after as possible, that ticket resellers have attempted to auction them off for hundreds of dollars, while some cinephiles have embarked on Homeric journeys to IMAX theaters multiple states away.

As such, this week’s competition for Dune: Part Three tickets renewed a feeling of stress and weariness among fans of Hollywood spectacle. Why, some asked, does catching a movie now feel as difficult as scoring tickets to a red-hot concert tour?

Adam Aron, CEO of AMC Theatres, took to his X account to apologize for the latest cinematic frustrations. (Reached for comment, the company directed WIRED to his comments on the platform.) “We thought we were ready, but we weren’t,” he wrote of the Dune launch, noting that the traffic surge to AMC’s website and mobile app was about triple the volume they’d seen for the latest Spider-Man installment.

“It’s a high-class problem to have such staggering demand, but even so it is intolerable and inexcusable,” Aron wrote. He further announced that $2 million in IT costs had been approved in order to “fully address the issue.”

Fandango and Regal Cinemas, whose apps and websites also drew complaints amid ongoing glitches, did not immediately return requests for comment. A representative for IMAX, which is not involved in ticket sales, declined to comment on the record. IMAX currently has more than 1,800 locations worldwide; in a quarterly financial update earlier this year, CEO Rich Gelfond said they saw the potential to double their footprint.

This depends, however, on exhibitors actively investing in more IMAX venues, as well as the availability of new or retrofitted auditoriums big enough for the screens and the theater architecture that goes along with them.

In the meantime, customer exasperation is mounting. Internet film critics bemoaned the “concertification” of movies as they contended with the same overloaded apps and long lines as everyone else.

“I'm done with the shenanigans of trying to be ‘FIRST’ to see these blockbuster films,” Simone Cromer, once known for her “Club Chalamet” fan accounts devoted to Dune star Timothée Chalamet, wrote on X. “I'll watch it on a regular screen sometime that week, without having to travel too far.”

Barry Hertz, film editor and chief film writer at The Globe and Mail, posted on X that vendors were failing the filmgoing public. “If you're going to turn movie ticket-buying into a competitive sport, then you need to have the tech and UX to support that shift,” he wrote.

Hertz tells WIRED that “eventizing” a movie “feels like a lifeline for theaters coming out of the depths of the pandemic,” and that there’s nothing inherently wrong with them encouraging audiences to pursue “a movie in its most ideal format” as they fight to maintain their bottom line.

“What can't happen, though, is theater owners forgetting that the rest of the experience has to be as easy and painless as possible,” Hertz continues. In his view, they haven’t lived up to this responsibility. “Don't add layers of technical frustration on top of a leisure activity that is fighting for its life.”

Stephanie Wang, a professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh who researches behavioral economics, suggests there are also significant social dimensions at play.

“Some consumers' desire for a ticket may be greater when they know both that many other people also want the ticket and cannot have it,” Wang tells WIRED. She points to an experiment published in The Review of Economic Studies in 2023 which found that “when some people are randomly excluded from being able to participate in an auction, the bids of those who are allowed to remain in the auction substantially increase.” Moreover, she adds, someone’s commitment to participating in the ultimate movie event can “signal to others, and sometimes to themselves as well, that they are true fans,” since it may “require you to give up time or sleep or something else of value.”

The potential solutions, alas, are not entirely obvious. Some members of the AMC Stubs A-List membership program this week suggested that they should have priority access to tickets at those theaters. But this ignores the economic reality of the subscription plan, which costs between $27.99 and $29.99 monthly and allows viewers to see up to four movies a week at no extra charge—including in formats like IMAX 70mm, a ticket which otherwise retails at $30 or more at AMC. In other words, outside of concessions, the chain isn’t making any additional money off A-Listers attending these premium screenings; the box-office take comes from the non-members paying full price.

“Of course, the classical economic question is, why don't the theaters just increase prices until supply equals demand and the market clears?” says Wang, identifying one theoretical way to cut down the secondary resale market. But, she says, theaters have reasons not to pull an audience that paid top dollar across the board. “They might want the fans who will give a rave review afterwards and spread the positive word in their social networks,” Wang explains, and those who sacrificed more for a ticket are more disposed to “believe that it's one of the best movies they have ever seen to justify the effort cost, which far exceeds the monetary cost.”

More likely, the chains and vendors will have to upgrade their tech, as AMC is already planning to do, and implement other guardrails to prevent a handful of users from snapping up as many tickets as they can to sell at a significant markup. Until they figure out those fixes, it seems that the battle for the best seats in the house will continue to be a bloodbath.

entries.title: The Best Digital Wall Calendar (2026): Skylight, Everblog, Apolosign
entries.summary: What originally looked like clutter turned out to be my new favorite gadget for organizing my family’s life.
entries.content:
I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.

I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was expensive and massive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using a digital wall calendar, but to my surprise, they have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.

These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.

Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here's everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they're right for you.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Skylight Buddy as a kid-friendly tool that includes some features of these digital calendar devices. I’ve also ensured accuracy and up-to-date information throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

My Favorite Digital Calendars

What’s a Digital Wall Calendar?

You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you've just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you're already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you've already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who's on the hook for which activities.

While these are often called wall calendars, you can usually choose to place them on a tabletop. I preferred the models that included a tabletop stand, but I was still able to prop up the ones that only came with wall-mounting hardware during my testing.

What Else Can a Digital Wall Calendar Do?

These devices aren't just calendars; they’re also designed for larger family management. You'll find features to help you plan meals, track to-do lists for multiple people, and earn rewards on a digital chore chart. The Skylight Calendar 2 is a favorite of mine because it includes a photo screensaver, but you'll need to be a Plus subscriber to get that and some of the other bonus features. Basically, you can use these calendars to manage your family's full schedule, chores, meals, and more in a single device.

Is a Digital Wall Calendar Worth It?

I didn't expect to feel this way, but having a physical version of my hyper-detailed Google Calendar in the center of my home has been a delight. My husband and I both check our calendar at a glance while we're chatting in the kitchen, and at the start of the week, we'll camp out in front of it for a few minutes to plan the week's dinners and grocery needs. My top pick, Skylight Calendar 2, actually prompts us to add items to our grocery list based on what meals we picked (if it's a stored recipe, that is).

My husband and I have found it so useful in part because we're both good about adding events to our individual calendars, so now this device can reflect that work. It lets us skip pulling out our phones when discussing plans for the next day or the upcoming weekend.

The Best Digital Calendars

Skylight's calendar is the most popular for a reason. The brand is known for its digital photo frames, and now you can use the same Skylight app to operate any of its three digital calendars: The older 10-inch Calendar ($170), the newer Calendar 2 ($320), and the Calendar Max ($630). The main difference between these is size, but Calendar 2 is the newest model, with improved performance and interchangeable Snap Frames ($30 to $50) you can purchase to change the device's look.

What makes Skylight great is its software. It's easy to use, and it quickly imported my Google Calendar and the wide variety of calendars shared to it, so I could immediately add all of my family's schedules to the device. The left-side menu bar shows all the pages you can toggle between. Calendar, Lists, Tasks, Rewards, Meals, and Recipes are the main areas you'll use; you can also access the Photos, Sleep, and Settings pages from the same menu.

The app and device interface are clean and intuitive compared with other models, many of which feel like Android tablets with a fancy calendar mode added. I was able to easily assign calendars I created on the device to family members. For example, I assigned my husband's calendar to him without needing him to log in or import it, and I could have assigned any calendar I created to my son as well. I also liked that shared events only appear once on the Skylight, but with both of our designated colors added to show the event in question applied to both of us.

Lists and Tasks sound similar, but Tasks are meant to function as a chore chart, connecting back to the Rewards page to build habits and earn the reward you set after hitting a certain goal. The main audience for this is children who are old enough to check the calendar. Lists are for things like your groceries. If you add recipes to the Recipe tab and then add those to your meal plan for that week, Skylight will offer to put the corresponding ingredients on your shopping list.

The downside of Skylight is the paywall. To access some of the best features—meal planning, rewards, photo screensaver, and the in-app AI assistant tool Sidekick—you'll need to be a Plus subscriber for either $79 a year or $8 a month. Having this device double as a digital photo frame makes it worth the cost to me. I love getting to have my two favorite things nearby: photos of my family and instant access to our shared calendars.

The Everblog HomeCal has an operating system that feels pleasantly similar to the Skylight. It has a bit of an Android undertone to it, but it doesn't feel like a giant tablet as much as the Apolosign or Cozyla calendars (both below). Setup was pretty seamless, but there was a delay for the device to update with my calendar invites. It would also take a while for the Everblog to reflect changes I made to my Google Calendar on another device. While it worked well for the most part during testing, I occasionally noticed events missing from my Everblog. It also turned each calendar email account I connected to the device into a separate profile, which was annoying. I could toggle off the extra emails when I was on pages outside of the calendar, though, so I didn't have three profiles for myself on my Chores page, for example.

The menu on the left-hand side is very similar to Skylight's, with options like Calendar, Chores, and Meal Plan. There isn't a recipe section, which I miss, but there is a Fridge section, which lets you track the groceries you already have. Part of why this exists is because Everblog also has a smaller, battery-powered version of this calendar that's designed to attach to your fridge, aptly named the FridgeCal ($249). Still, I prefer the Recipe tab on the Skylight. The Everblog also has a Chores tab, but no additional tab for tracking regular chores or other to-dos separately.

There's a free photo option, but the uploader tool in the app only lets you add one photo at a time. Painful, but I'm sure many would feel it's worth the free price tag. To use the feature, you'll need to go into the settings on the physical device to turn on photo slideshow as your screensaver. The Everblog defaults to pinging loudly at the start of any calendar event, which you can only change on the device, not in the app.

There's a button on the bottom right-hand corner of the screen that will take you to a homepage with an overview of the calendar and chores, and access to other applications like Spotify and Netflix, if you set up your accounts on this device for streaming content. It comes enabled for wall mounting, but you can purchase the Calendar Stand ($39) if you want to situate it on a tabletop, and there's a wooden frame ($99) you can buy to snap on to give it a nicer look.

Apolosign's digital calendar has three sizes: 15.7, 21.5, and 27 inches. It runs Google's Android OS, so it operates very similarly to an Android tablet and to Google's Pixel Tablet, if you've used either as a smart display, as I have. The Apolosign has two modes: Calendar and Android. Calendar mode worked similarly to Skylight. I seamlessly connected it to my Google Calendar, imported over most of my various shared calendars, and color-coded them.

The Calendar mode has a left-side menu bar (you'll have to tap to make it appear), with sections for Home, Calendar, Routines, To-Dos, Rewards, and Meals. The Home page has a two-column design, showing you the calendar on one side and your Routines and To-Dos on the other. You can then tap into any of these sections or check off items directly from the Home page. Apolosign also has baked-in notifications that chime to remind you about calendar events and to-dos, plus phone notifications to let you know how many items are on your calendar that day.

WIRED Reviewer Kat Merck also tested Apolosign, but used Android mode instead of Calendar mode. Android mode allows you to customize widgets and layout, so she opted for a monthly view. This mode also lets you use photos from Google Photos as a background and screensaver. She says it's nice to be able to customize the layout in this mode, but it struggles to sync with other programs, including Apolosign's own app.

I don't like the Apolosign experience quite as much as the Skylight or Everblog, and Kat agreed that this device is not very intuitive and takes a lot of patience to set up. But having no paywall is a huge plus, and many people will feel it's worth getting used to the more Android-style experience to not pay a monthly or yearly fee. But since it's essentially a large Android tablet, iPhone users have flagged on Reddit that they can't two-way sync between it and their iPhone devices. The Apolosign is often on sale for the same price, if not cheaper, than the Skylight.

If you want a version made for kids, Skylight has something along those lines called the Skylight Buddy (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It's not a digital calendar but rather a chore-and-routine display that helps kids visualize and check off their daily to-dos without needing to navigate an entire family calendar.

My 4-year-old loves his 7-inch Buddy, and it really does help get him to brush his teeth and put on his PJs in a timely (well, more timely) fashion now that it's in his room. It also has a night-light and sound machine, but the sounds are limited, and the night-light is pretty dim. So for those capabilities, I'm sticking to the Hatch Baby my son is used to and loves.

Ultimately, this is most useful if you already have and use a Skylight Calendar. That’s because the Buddy can sync to and show designated tasks already on the Skylight Calendar. But even if you don't have the Calendar and just want more of a routine tool or chore-tracker for your child, this is a really good option. There are subscription options to get more features—Buddy Plus is $39 a year, and Skylight Plus is $79 a year. Skylight Plus is what you should get if you have the Calendar, as it unlocks paywalled features for both devices. But I haven't needed any subscription-only capabilities to keep my son excited about and engaged in his bedtime routine.

Others I’ve Tested

Cozyla Calendar Plus 2 (15.6 Inches) for $350: This calendar is similar to Apolosign with an Android-based operating system, but it didn't import my shared calendars, meaning it took more work to set up. It was overall frustrating to navigate and didn't guide me through its tools as effectively as Skylight or Apolosign. While Cozyla doesn't have any subscription fees, its 15.6-inch size is more expensive than both Skylight's and Apolosign's.

Hearth Display for $699: This is another digital calendar and family tool that has a paywall with an affordable Family Membership ($6 a month) but a much higher initial price point. It's only available in a large, 27-inch size, and I found it was slow to load my calendar and also bulky compared to more affordable options.

FAQs

How Do Digital Wall Calendars Work?

Digital wall calendars sync with your existing digital calendar app of choice, like Google Calendar, and display it on the physical screen. There are usually additional tools for recipes, to-do lists, and chores, but each digital wall calendar varies in how you import the information. You may have to manually import it or type the details into the device, but once you get used to the process, the function can be helpful for the whole family.

Will Changes to My Calendar Appear Instantly?

Changes you make on your native calendar app, like Google Calendar and Apple's Calendar, should reflect quickly onto the digital wall calendar device. But changes you make on the device aren't always backward compatible with the native calendar. It depends on the calendar's settings and how the information was shared; I can edit my primary personal calendar on the Skylight Calendar 2, for example, but I can’t edit my work calendar that I shared to the Skylight through my personal. There are also some syncing issues you may run into with the Apolosign, which doesn't two-way sync with an iPhone since the digital calendar runs on an Android operating system.

How Is a Digital Calendar Different From a Smart Display?

Many smart displays look similar to these devices but have an entirely different operating system. Sure, the Google Pixel Tablet has some overlap with the Apolosign and Cozyla, since they all run an Android operating system. But unlike smart displays, digital calendar devices are designed with specific tools to run your family and none of the clutter. You'll lose out on smart-home support, though Apolosign claims you can use Google Assistant on it (that hasn't worked for me so far). On most devices, you'll also compromise on extras like video streaming (you can, however, stream on Everblog). But as someone who uses a smart display regularly, I really didn’t miss it once I switched over to the digital calendar device. I do wish there were a weather-report page, as most digital wall calendars just show the current weather.

Does It Have to Go on the Wall?

No—in fact, most of these devices come with a table-stand option. I only tested in table-stand mode since I had multiple of these devices in my house at one time, but the wall-mounting option is nice, allowing you to keep your tabletops clear. The 15-inch models are great for tabletops, and you may want to consider larger sizes for the wall-mounting route.
